title: Shalom Aleichem
hook: the Friday night song welcomes angels; the Talmud says two walk you home (Shabbat 119b)
tomorrow: a guest at the Friday table

segments.voice: Yesterday, tkhines, the women's prayers said at the candles: light, cover, bless, then look. Your line was eyes closed, the week ends. And this is day one hundred. A hundred days. That's worth a breath on its own.

Friday night, the walk home from synagogue. The streets are quieter than usual. Somebody has a child on their shoulders. Maybe it's cold, maybe it's warm and you can hear other families' dinners through open windows. You open your door: the candles are already burning, the table is set. And before anyone sits down, the family stands around the table and starts to sing. Not to each other. To guests nobody can see.
screen: `THE WALK HOME ON FRIDAY NIGHT.` → `THE CANDLES ARE BURNING.` → `A SONG FOR GUESTS NO ONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Shalom aleichem means peace be upon you. It's also an everyday greeting, a hello in Hebrew and Yiddish. But on Friday night it's a song, sung to angels. The idea comes from a story in the Talmud. Two ministering angels, it says, walk a person home from synagogue on Friday night, one good and one bad. If the candles are lit, the table is set and the beds are made, the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat too. And the bad angel has no choice but to answer amen. If the house is dark and nothing's ready, it goes the other way around, and the good angel has to say amen. It's a story about habit: the way you welcome this week shapes the next. The song is much younger than the story. Tradition traces it to Kabbalist circles, many centuries after the Talmud. It has four short verses, often each sung three times. Welcome, angels of peace. Come in peace. Bless me with peace. Go in peace. Some people ask, reasonably, why you'd tell angels to leave. One answer is simple courtesy: they walked you home, and now you can let them go. Another is that the family is about to sit down together, and some moments are just for the people at the table. Families sing it to many tunes, fast and slow. Some hold hands. Some sing it once, quietly, alone. It turns an ordinary doorway into the place where the week's peace comes in.
screen: `PEACE BE UPON YOU.` · `TWO ANGELS WALK YOU HOME.` · `MAY IT BE LIKE THIS NEXT TIME.` · `WELCOME, COME, BLESS, GO IN PEACE.` · then, large: `THE DOORWAY WHERE PEACE COMES IN.`

segments.voice: Picture the next door you'll walk through, home, work, a friend's place, and your hand on it. Pick any tune that feels like peace to you and hum a little of it, even under your breath. Picture walking through that door humming, with two quiet companions beside you, noticing what kind of place you've made.
Shalom Aleichem. Peace be upon you: a greeting, and the Friday night song that welcomes the angels of peace home.
Your line: angels walk you home. Come in peace, go in peace. That's day one hundred.
